context.full_target:
A sphere-valued map cannot vanish outside a compact set. As approved by
the user on 2026-10-23, interpret spatial compact support as compact support
of a perturbation from a **fixed unit vector**, locally uniformly in time.
This is a disclosed nontrivial interpretation, not a claimed author-issued
correction.

Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
\(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:

1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
   \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
   \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
   assumed.
3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
   \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
   \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).

With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define

\[
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
\qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
\]

The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
\(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.
context.conclusion: For every real t>0, e(·,t) is Lebesgue integrable on ℝ^n, E is differentiable at t, and E'(t)=0. Moreover E(s)=E(t) for all real s,t>0. The energy is exactly ∫_{ℝ^n} (|u_t|²+Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|²) dx, without a factor 1/2; no conclusion at time zero is asserted.

record.definition: Ω=ℝ^n × (0,∞), the domain of u, with the relative Euclidean smooth structure.

record.type: partial differentiation notation on the open domain Ω
record.definition: ∂ denotes ordinary coordinate partial differentiation, component by component for vector-valued functions. Subscripts t and tt denote one and two time derivatives, x_j and x_jx_j denote one and two derivatives in spatial coordinate j, and x_jt denotes first time then spatial differentiation. Thus u_t=∂_t u, u_tt=∂_t∂_t u and ∂_{x_j}u_t=∂_{x_j}∂_t u. The same notation applies to any differentiable real scalar function. Derivatives are used only where their existence has been established. For native total-function source applications, a function on Ω may be extended by zero outside Ω; at points of Ω all derivatives refer to its germ on Ω, independent of the extension.

record.type: spatial Laplacian on vector-valued twice differentiable functions on Ω

record.definition: e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|²+Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u(x,t)|². All norms are Euclidean; the spatial sum is the Frobenius square of the spatial gradient.

E(t)=∫_{ℝ^n}e(x,t) dx for t>0. For definiteness this is the total real Bochner integral convention (zero if not integrable); the proof separately proves integrability for every t>0, so the intended ordinary finite Lebesgue integral is obtained.

record.type: Lebesgue measure and integration notation on finite real coordinate spaces
record.definition: dx is standard Lebesgue measure on ℝ^n, identified with the finite product of one-dimensional Lebesgue measures in standard coordinates. On other real coordinate spaces the same notation means their standard Lebesgue measure, including mass one on the zero-dimensional space. Integrable means measurable with finite integral of the absolute value. A set indicator 1_A is 1 on A and 0 elsewhere, for any set A in the integration space.
v·w=dot(v,w)=Σ_{k=1}^d v_k w_k for v,w∈ℝ^d and any finite dimension d; |v|²=v·v.
